title: Santa Claus Conquers the Martians

evidence.note: Renewal absence cannot make this 1964 film public domain. For a work first published in 1964, 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) says a renewal application 'is not a condition of the renewal and extension of the copyright', so the renewal term attaches automatically. Public domain would have to rest on a missing copyright notice on the 1964 release prints, and I could not verify that from any source I fetched. Wikipedia and Plagiarism Today say the film is public domain in the US but do not document the basis.

Sound film. The recorded soundtrack normally shares the film's status, so it is undetermined for the same reason as the print. Wikipedia credits the music to Milton DeLugg. I did not verify any separate music copyright or registration.

Wikipedia credits the story to Glenville Mareth and the screenplay to Paul L. Jacobson, so this looks like an original screenplay rather than an adaptation of an older published work. I did not find any separate publication or registration of the story, so the story layer follows the print and is undetermined.

Plagiarism Today says that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds the copyright and enforces it. I did not confirm any specific restoration or its added material. Any cleaned-up transfer, new titles or added commentary would be protectable even if the underlying print were free.

renewal_search.negative_result: Not run. Renewal is not the controlling question for a 1964 work under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so a renewal-absence search would not establish public domain status here.

editorial:
Santa Claus Conquers the Martians is a 1964 American children's science-fiction comedy directed by Nicholas Webster, with John Call as Santa Claus. Martian leaders fear their children have gone lazy and joyless from watching Earth TV, so they abduct Santa. Wikipedia credits the story to Glenville Mareth, the screenplay to Paul L. Jacobson, the music to Milton DeLugg and the US release to Embassy Pictures on November 14, 1964, on an estimated $200,000 budget. It became a cult title and was featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000 in 1991.

The rights trap is the shortcut that an old film was never renewed. A film published in 1964 got its renewal term automatically under 17 U.S.C. 304(a), so renewal does not decide this one. It would have to be free for another reason, such as a missing notice, and I found no document establishing that. Secondary sources call it public domain in the US only, and Plagiarism Today says STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces rights abroad. Check the notice on an actual print before reusing it, and keep it out of non-US distribution.
faq: Is Santa Claus Conquers the Martians public domain because the copyright was not renewed?

That reason does not work for a 1964 film. Under 17 U.S.C. 304(a)(3)(B) a renewal application is not a condition of the renewal term, so the term attaches automatically. The film could be public domain in the US only through a defect such as a missing copyright notice. I could not verify one, so the status is undetermined here.
Can I use the Internet Archive copy, including outside the US?

The Internet Archive copy is a community upload carrying the uploader's Public Domain Mark; I have not verified its source or quality beyond its metadata. Plagiarism Today reports that outside the US, STUDIOCANAL holds and enforces the copyright. For anything beyond US use, get a clearance first.
